---bf:Tb3b,### A. Strength & Appointment (Articles 216 & 217)
- **Strength Determination**: Unlike the Supreme Court where Parliament fixes the sanctioned strength by law, the Constitution leaves the strength of a High Court flexible:
  $$\text{Strength of a High Court is determined by the } \mathbf{PRESIDENT\text{ OF INDIA}} \text{ based on workload.}$$
- **Mode of Appointment (Article 217(1))**:
  - Appointed by the **President of India**.
  - **Chief Justice of High Court**: Appointed after consultation with the **Chief Justice of India (CJI)** and the **Governor of the State**.
  - **Other High Court Judges**: Appointed after consultation with the CJI, the Governor of the State, and the **Chief Justice of the concerned High Court**.
- **The High Court Collegium Mechanism**:
  1. Proposal initiates from the **High Court Collegium** (Chief Justice of HC + 2 senior-most HC judges).
  2. Forwarded to the Governor/Chief Minister, who transmits it to the Union Law Minister.
  3. The Union Law Minister submits it to the **Supreme Court Collegium** (CJI + 2 senior-most Supreme Court judges).
  4. The CJI consults two Supreme Court colleagues conversant with that particular High Court before tendering recommendations to the President.

---

### B. Qualifications for Appointment (Article 217(2))
A person must be a **Citizen of India**, and must satisfy **ANY ONE** of the following:
1. Has for at least **ten years held a judicial office** in the territory of India; **OR**
2. Has for at least **ten years been an advocate of a High Court** (or of two or more such courts in succession).
- > [!WARNING]
  > **EXAM TRAP: No "Distinguished Jurist" for High Courts**
  > While a distinguished jurist can be appointed as a Supreme Court Judge under Article 124(3)(c), there is **NO provision for appointing a distinguished jurist to a High Court** under Article 217(2)!

---

### C. Oath, Tenure, Removal & Transfer (Articles 217, 219, 222)
- **Oath (Article 219)**: Administered by the **Governor of the State** (or person appointed by him).
- **Tenure**: Retires at the age of **62 years** (raised from 60 to 62 by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963). (Supreme Court retirement age is 65).
- **Resignation**: Addressed in writing to the **President of India** (NOT the Governor!).
- **Removal**: Removed by the President in the **same manner and on the same grounds (proved misbehaviour or incapacity) as a Supreme Court Judge** (Article 217(1) Proviso (b) cross-referencing Article 124(4)).
- **Transfer of High Court Judges (Article 222)**:
  - President transfers a judge after consultation with the CJI.
  - In the *Third Judges Case (1998)*, SC ruled that CJI must consult: (1) Collegium of 4 senior-most SC judges, (2) CJ of the High Court from which the judge is being transferred, and (3) CJ of the High Court to which the judge is being transferred.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Supervisory Jurisdiction under Article 227**:
> The High Court has **superintendence over all courts and tribunals** throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction.
> - Covers both **administrative and judicial superintendence**.
> - Can be exercised *suo motu* (not dependent on appeal).
> - **The Sole Exclusion (Article 227(4))**: Does not apply to courts or tribunals constituted by or under any law relating to the **Armed Forces (Courts Martial)**.

### Appointments in the Subordinate Judiciary:
1. **District Judges (Article 233)**:
   - Appointed, posted, and promoted by the **Governor of the State in consultation with the High Court**.
   - *Eligibility for Direct Recruitment*: A person who has been an advocate or a pleader for **not less than seven (7) years** and is recommended by the High Court.
2. **Other Judicial Officers (Article 234)**:
   - Appointed by the **Governor** in accordance with rules made by him after consultation with the **State Public Service Commission (SPSC)** and the **High Court**.
3. **Control over Subordinate Courts (Article 235)**:
   - The posting, promotion, grant of leave, and disciplinary control over judicial officers is vested **exclusively in the High Court** to ensure separation of powers from the executive.

---c2:T1243,### A. The Constitutional Mandate: Article 39A
Inserted by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976**, Article 39A directs the State to secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity, and to provide **free legal aid** by suitable legislation or schemes.

---

### B. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
Established a statutory hierarchy to deliver free and competent legal services to the underprivileged:
1. **National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)**:
   - **Patron-in-Chief**: Chief Justice of India.
   - **Executive Chairman**: A serving or retired Judge of the Supreme Court appointed by the President.
2. **State Legal Services Authority (SLSA)**:
   - Headed by the **Chief Justice of the High Court** as Patron-in-Chief.
   - Executive Chairman is a serving or retired High Court Judge nominated by the Governor.
3. **District Legal Services Authority (DLSA)**:
   - Headed by the **District Judge** as Chairman.
4. **Taluk Legal Services Committee**:
   - Headed by a Senior Civil Judge.

---

### C. Lok Adalats (People's Courts)
Lok Adalats are statutory alternative dispute resolution forums established under Chapter VI of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
- **Composition**: Presiding Officer (sitting or retired judicial officer) + a practicing advocate + a social worker.
- **Jurisdiction**:
  1. Any case pending before any court.
  2. Any dispute at the pre-litigation stage.
  - *Subject Matters Covered*: Matrimonial disputes, land partition, motor accident claims, bank recovery, labour disputes, and **compoundable criminal offences**. (Non-compoundable criminal offences **cannot** be settled by Lok Adalats!).

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   THE UNIQUE LEGAL NATURE OF A LOK ADALAT AWARD                                  │
├────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ STATUTORY STATUS   │ Every award made by a Lok Adalat is DEEMED TO BE A DECREE OF A CIVIL COURT   │
│ (SECTION 21)       │ or an order of any other court.                                             │
├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ FINALITY & BAR     │ The award is FINAL AND BINDING ON ALL PARTIES to the dispute.               │
│ ON APPEALS         │ NO APPEAL LIES TO ANY COURT against the award of a Lok Adalat!              │
├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ REFUND OF COURT    │ Where a pending case is settled by a Lok Adalat, the COURT FEES PAID ARE     │
│ FEES               │ REFUNDED in full to the parties under the Court Fees Act, 1870.             │
└────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### D. Permanent Lok Adalats (2002 Amendment)
- Established under **Section 22B** of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (inserted by 2002 Amendment).
- Exclusively dedicated to **Public Utility Services (PUS)**: postal, telegraph, telephone, power, light, water supply, public conservancy, sanitation, hospitals, passenger/goods transport, insurance.
- **Pecuniary Jurisdiction**: Up to **₹1 Crore** (enhanced from earlier limits).
- **Adjudicatory Power**: If the parties fail to reach an amicable settlement, the Permanent Lok Adalat has the power to **decide the dispute on merits** (unlike ordinary Lok Adalats which can only mediate).
- Its award is final, binding, and non-appealable.

---c3:T652,```
Q1. How is the sanctioned strength of a High Court determined under the Constitution, and how does 
    it differ from the Supreme Court?
A1. The strength of a High Court is determined by the PRESIDENT OF INDIA based on workload under 
    Article 216. In contrast, the strength of the Supreme Court is determined by PARLIAMENT BY LAW 
    under Article 124(1).

Q2. What is the retirement age of a High Court judge, and which constitutional amendment raised it 
    from 60 to 62?
A2. 62 years of age. It was increased from 60 to 62 by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963.

Q3. In what key respect is the writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226 broader than that 
    of the Supreme Court under Article 32?
A3. Under Article 32, the Supreme Court can issue writs ONLY for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights 
    (Part III). Under Article 226, the High Court can issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental 
    Rights AND "FOR ANY OTHER PURPOSE" (ordinary legal rights).

Q4. Can a death sentence awarded by a Sessions Judge be executed immediately?
A4. No. Under Section 366 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (and Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita), 
    any death sentence passed by a Sessions Court MUST BE CONFIRMED BY THE HIGH COURT before it can 
    be executed.

Q5. Can an appeal be filed in a High Court against the award passed by a statutory Lok Adalat?
A5. No. Under Section 21 of the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987, the award of a Lok Adalat is 
    deemed a civil court decree and is final and binding on all parties; NO APPEAL lies to any court 
    against it.

---c5:T898,In classical Anglo-Saxon jurisprudence, courts operated on the model of a **passive arbiter**, waiting for an aggrieved individual with personal injury to initiate proceedings and strictly confining relief to inter-party disputes.
In the late 1970s—following the trauma of the Internal Emergency (1975–1977) where the judiciary had capitulated in *ADM Jabalpur*—the Supreme Court of India underwent a profound institutional metamorphosis:
- It transformed itself from a **court of law for the affluent** into a **court of justice for the downtrodden**.
- This paradigm shift was catalyzed by two visionary jurists: **Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer** and **Justice P.N. Bhagwati**.
- **Coined Origin**: The term *Judicial Activism* was originally coined in the United States in 1947 by the American historian and author **Arthur Schlesinger Jr.** in a *Fortune* magazine article.

```
                      THE PARADIGM SHIFT IN INDIAN JURISPRUDENCE
                      
      [TRADITIONAL JURISPRUDENCE]                   [ACTIVIST JURISPRUDENCE]
 ┌───────────────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────────────────┐

---c6:T7b3,### A. Meaning & Conceptual Core
**Public Interest Litigation (PIL)** means litigation undertaken for the protection and advancement of the public interest. Unlike traditional adversarial litigation where one party sues another for private vindication, PIL is collaborative:
> *"PIL is not litigation of an adversarial character undertaken by one person against another. It is a challenge and an opportunity to the government and its officers to make basic human rights meaningful to the deprived and vulnerable sections of the community."*
> — **Justice P.N. Bhagwati in *Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984)***

---

### B. The Demolition of Traditional *Locus Standi*
- **The Traditional Rule**: Only the person whose legal or constitutional rights were directly infringed possessed the standing (*locus standi*) to invoke the writ jurisdiction of the court.
- **The PIL Revolution**: Where a legal wrong or injury is caused to a person or class of persons who, by reason of **poverty, helplessness, disability, or social/economic disadvantage**, cannot approach the court for relief, **any public-spirited citizen, advocate, or social organization can maintain an application for an appropriate direction, order, or writ under Article 32 or Article 226**.

---

### C. The Doctrine of Epistolary Jurisdiction
- Courts dispensed with procedural technicalities: formal affidavits, stamp duties, and structured petition drafts were no longer mandatory.
- **Epistolary Jurisdiction**: The Supreme Court and High Courts began treating **simple letters, postcards, telegrams, and newspaper clippings** addressed to the Chief Justice or individual judges as formal writ petitions!
- *Landmark Inception*: In *Sunil Batra (II) v. Delhi Administration (1980)*, a prisoner in Tihar Jail scribbled a letter on a scrap of paper describing the brutal torture inflicted on a fellow prisoner. Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer converted that piece of paper into a habeas corpus writ petition.

---c9:Ta81,The democratization of judicial access led to rampant opportunism. PIL began degenerating into:
- **"Private Interest Litigation"**: Settling personal commercial vendettas.
- **"Publicity Interest Litigation"**: Frivolous filings by lawyers seeking media headlines.
- **"Politics Interest Litigation"**: Opposition parties using courts to fight political battles lost on the legislative floor.

### Guidelines in *State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010)*:
To prevent the abuse of PIL, a 3-judge bench laid down binding directives for High Courts and the Supreme Court:
1. Courts must encourage genuine and bona fide PIL and curb petitions filed for extraneous motivations.
2. The court must verify the **credentials and antecedents of the petitioner** before entertaining a PIL.
3. The court must ensure that the petition involves **substantial public interest** affecting a large section of society.
4. Courts must verify whether there is an alternative remedy available before accepting the PIL.
5. Frivolous and vexatious petitions filed with oblique motives must be rejected with **exemplary costs** imposed on the petitioner.

---cb:T7e6,```
Q1. Who was the advocate that filed the first reported Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India, 
    and what was the subject matter of the case?
A1. Pushpa Kapila Hingorani (known as the "Mother of PIL") filed Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, 
    State of Bihar (1979), highlighting the plight of undertrial prisoners languishing in Bihar jails. 
    It led to the release of over 40,000 undertrials.

Q2. What is "Epistolary Jurisdiction" in the context of Indian constitutional law?
A2. It is the procedural innovation whereby the Supreme Court and High Courts treat simple letters, 
    postcards, or telegrams addressed by citizens or prisoners to judges as formal writ petitions, 
    waiving the requirement of formal drafting, fees, and affidavits.

Q3. In which landmark case did the Supreme Court replace the 1868 British doctrine of Strict Liability 
    with the doctrine of Absolute Liability?
A3. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), commonly known as the Oleum Gas Leak Case, where the 
    court held that enterprises engaged in hazardous activities owe an absolute, non-delegable duty 
    to the community with zero exceptions.

Q4. What guidelines did the Supreme Court issue in State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010)?
A4. The 3-judge bench laid down comprehensive guidelines to curb frivolous, politically motivated, 
    and extortionate PILs, directing courts to verify petitioner antecedents, ensure substantial public 
    interest, and impose exemplary costs on frivolous filings.

Q5. What is the fundamental difference between Judicial Activism and Judicial Overreach?
A5. Judicial Activism involves the court compelling the executive or legislature to fulfill their 
    constitutional obligations in the face of policy inertia or rights violations. Judicial Overreach 
    occurs when the judiciary crosses constitutional boundaries to substitute its own wisdom for 
    executive policymaking, enters administrative management, or usurps legislative drafting.

---cd:T17d0,In Indian administrative law, state institutions are classified into three epistemic tiers:
1. **Constitutional Bodies**: Established directly by explicit articles of the Constitution of India. Any alteration in their structure, powers, or tenure mandates a formal Constitutional Amendment under **Article 368** (e.g., ECI, CAG, UPSC, Finance Commission, GST Council).
2. **Statutory Bodies**: Created by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature. Can be modified or dissolved through ordinary legislative enactments (e.g., NHRC, SEBI, NGT, Lokpal).
3. **Executive / Extra-Constitutional Bodies**: Created through an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet without statutory backing (e.g., NITI Aayog).

---ce:T1867,### A. Composition & Evolution of the Multi-Member Structure
- **Article 324(2)**: The Election Commission consists of the **Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)** and such number of other **Election Commissioners (ECs)**, if any, as the President may from time to time fix.
- **Evolutionary Trajectory**:
  $$\text{1950–1989: Single-Member} \longrightarrow \text{Oct 1989: Multi-Member (1+2)} \longrightarrow \text{1990: Single-Member} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Oct\text{ 1993–Present: 3-Member (1+2)}}$$
- **The Equality Principle (*T.N. Seshan v. Union of India, 1995*)**:
  The Supreme Court affirmed that the Chief Election Commissioner and the two other Election Commissioners have **equal powers, draw identical salaries (equivalent to a Supreme Court Judge)**, and in case of difference of opinion, matters are decided by **majority vote**. The CEC is merely *primus inter pares* (first among equals) inside the commission.

---

### B. Appointment Architecture: The 2023 Statutory Transformation
- **The Pre-2023 Status**: Appointed unilaterally by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister/Cabinet.
- ***Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023)* (5-Judge Constitution Bench)**:
  The Supreme Court ruled that to preserve electoral democracy, until Parliament enacted a law, appointments must be made by the President on the recommendation of a Committee consisting of:
  $$\text{SC Benchmark: } \mathbf{Prime\text{ Minister}} + \mathbf{Leader\text{ of Opposition in Lok Sabha}} + \mathbf{Chief\text{ Justice of India}}$$
- **The Statutory Framework (*The Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners Act, 2023*)**:
  Parliament enacted a statute replacing the CJI with a Union Cabinet Minister:
  1. **Search Committee**: Headed by the **Minister of Law and Justice** and two other members not below the rank of Secretary to GOI; prepares a panel of 5 candidates.
  2. **Selection Committee**:
     - **Prime Minister** (Chairperson)
     - **Leader of Opposition (or Leader of the Single Largest Opposition Party) in Lok Sabha**
     - **A Union Cabinet Minister** nominated by the Prime Minister.
  3. The President appoints the CEC and ECs on the recommendation of this Selection Committee.

---

> [!WARNING]
> **EXAM TRAP: Municipal & Panchayat Elections**
> The Election Commission of India has **zero jurisdiction** over elections to Panchayats and Municipalities. Local elections are conducted exclusively by the **State Election Commission** constituted under **Articles 243K and 243ZA**. ECI conducts elections strictly for: (1) Parliament, (2) State Legislatures, (3) President of India, and (4) Vice-President of India.

---cf:Tbd0,Dr. B.R. Ambedkar declared in the Constituent Assembly:
> *"The Comptroller and Auditor General of India shall be the most important officer under the Constitution of India. He is one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system of government in India (the others being the Supreme Court, UPSC, and Election Commission)."*

### A. Appointment, Oath & Tenure (Article 148)
- Appointed by the **President of India by warrant under his hand and seal**.
- **Tenure**: Holds office for a term of **six (6) years or until attaining the age of 65 years**, whichever is earlier.
- **Oath**: Administered by the President under the **Third Schedule**: to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the Constitution and laws without fear or favour.
- **Removal**: Removed by the President in the **same manner and on the same grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court** (proved misbehaviour or incapacity via Article 368 special majority in Parliament).

---

### B. Constitutional Independence Guarantees (Article 148)
1. **Security of Tenure**: Does not hold office during the pleasure of the President.
2. **Ineligibility for Further Office (Article 148(4))**:
   $$\text{CAG is strictly } \mathbf{INELIGIBLE} \text{ for further office under the Government of India or any State.}$$
3. **Salary Protection (Article 148(6))**: Administrative expenses of the office of CAG (salaries, pensions, allowances) are **charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India** (non-votable by Parliament).
4. Service conditions cannot be varied to his disadvantage after appointment.

---

### C. Duties, Audit Scope & Relationship with PAC (Articles 149–151)
- Under the *CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971*:
  - Audits all receipts and expenditure from the **Consolidated Fund of India**, the Consolidated Fund of each State, and each Union Territory having a legislative assembly.
  - Audits all transactions relating to the **Contingency Funds** and **Public Accounts** of the Union and States.
  - Audits all trading, manufacturing, profit and loss accounts of government departments.
  - Audits all Government Companies under the *Companies Act, 2013* and corporations established by parliamentary law.
- **Audit Reports (Article 151)**:
  - Submits **three audit reports** to the President relating to Union accounts:
    1. *Audit Report on Appropriation Accounts*
    2. *Audit Report on Finance Accounts*
    3. *Audit Report on Public Undertakings*
  - The President causes them to be laid before both Houses of Parliament.
  - These reports are examined by the **Public Accounts Committee (PAC)**; CAG acts as the **"friend, philosopher, and guide" of the PAC**.
- **Regulatory Audit vs. Propriety Audit**:
  - *Regulatory Audit*: Verifies that moneys shown in accounts were legally available, authorized, and expended according to rules.
  - *Propriety Audit*: Examines the wisdom, faithfulness, and economy of government expenditure to check whether public funds were wasted or mismanaged.

### B. Removal Procedure: The Binding Supreme Court Reference (Article 317)
- The President can remove the Chairman or any member of UPSC / SPSC directly on grounds of: (1) Insolvency, (2) Paid employment outside duties, or (3) Infirmity of mind or body.
- **On Ground of "Misbehaviour" (Article 317(1))**:
  - The President **MUST refer the matter to the Supreme Court of India** for an inquiry.
  - If the Supreme Court, after inquiry, advises that the Chairman or member ought to be removed, **the President MUST remove them**.
  - **The Advice of the Supreme Court is STRICTLY BINDING on the President!**

---

### C. Post-Tenure Ineligibility Grid (Article 319)

```

---d1:T86c,### A. Nature & Composition
- A **quasi-judicial body** constituted by the President of India **every fifth year**, or at such earlier time as the President considers necessary.
- **Composition (Finance Commission Act, 1951)**:
  - Consists of a **Chairman and four other members** appointed by the President.
  - *Chairman*: Experienced in public affairs.
  - *4 Members Qualifications*:
    1. A Judge of a High Court or qualified to be appointed as such.
    2. A person with specialized knowledge of finance and accounts of the Government.
    3. A person with wide experience in financial matters and administration.
    4. A person with special knowledge of economics.

---

### B. Four Core Constitutional Functions (Article 280(3))
1. **Vertical Devolution**: The distribution between the Union and the States of the net proceeds of taxes which are to be, or may be, divided between them under Chapter I of Part XII.
2. **Horizontal Allocation**: The allocation between the States of the respective shares of such tax proceeds.
3. **Grants-in-Aid Principles**: The principles that should govern the grants-in-aid of the revenues of the States out of the Consolidated Fund of India under **Article 275**.
4. **Panchayat & Municipal Resource Augmentation**:
   - Under **Article 280(3)(bb)**: Measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of the **Panchayats** on the basis of recommendations made by the State Finance Commission.
   - Under **Article 280(3)(c)**: Measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of the **Municipalities** on the basis of recommendations made by the State Finance Commission.

> [!NOTE]
> **Advisory Character**: The recommendations made by the Finance Commission are purely **advisory** in nature and not legally binding on the Government of India. However, successive governments have followed the convention of accepting devolution formulas.
> - *15th Finance Commission (N.K. Singh)*: Recommended **41% vertical devolution** to States for 2021–2026 (adjusted downward by 1% from 42% to account for J&K and Ladakh UT status).

---d2:T498,Inserted by the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016**, the GST Council is a joint constitutional forum for the Centre and States.
- **Composition**:
  - Chairperson: **Union Finance Minister**
  - Member: **Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance**
  - Members: **Ministers in charge of Finance or Taxation** of each State Government.
  - Vice-Chairperson: Chosen by and from amongst the State Ministers.
- **Decision-Making & Weighted Voting Formula (Article 279A(9))**:
  - **Quorum**: Minimum **one-half (50%)** of the total number of members.
  - **Passage Majority**: Every decision is taken by a majority of **NOT LESS THAN THREE-FOURTHS (3/4th / 75%) of the weighted votes** of the members present and voting.
  - **Weighted Allocation**:
    $$\text{Vote of the Central Government} = \frac{1}{3}\text{rd (33.33\%) of the Total Votes Cast}$$
    $$\text{Votes of ALL State Governments Combined} = \frac{2}{3}\text{rds (66.67\%) of the Total Votes Cast}$$
  - *Federal Equilibrium*: Neither the Centre alone (33%) nor all States combined (67%) can pass a resolution unilaterally without a degree of cross-consensus to cross the 75% threshold!

> [!CAUTION]
> **Solicitor General of India**:
> In addition to the AG, there is a Solicitor General of India and Additional Solicitors General to assist the AG.
> **EXAM TRAP**: The offices of the Solicitor General and Additional Solicitor General are **NOT constitutional offices**; they are not mentioned in Article 76. Only the Attorney General is a constitutional office.

---d5:T7aa,```
Q1. Under what circumstance is the President of India constitutionally bound to accept the advice 
    tendered by the Supreme Court regarding the removal of an SPSC member?
A1. Under Article 317(1), when an SPSC or UPSC Chairman/Member is sought to be removed on the ground 
    of "misbehaviour", the President must refer the case to the Supreme Court for an inquiry. The 
    advice rendered by the Supreme Court after that inquiry is STRICTLY BINDING on the President.

Q2. What is the voting weightage distribution in the GST Council under Article 279A(9)?
A2. The vote of the Central Government has a weightage of ONE-THIRD (33.33%) of the total votes cast; 
    the votes of all State Governments taken together have a weightage of TWO-THIRDS (66.67%) of the 
    total votes cast. Decisions require a 3/4th (75%) weighted majority.

Q3. What makes the removal of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) independent of the Union Cabinet?
A3. Under Article 148(1), the CAG can be removed ONLY in the same manner and on the same grounds as a 
    Judge of the Supreme Court (proved misbehaviour or incapacity, supported by a Special Majority 
    under Article 368 in both Houses of Parliament). He does not serve during the pleasure of the President.

Q4. Why is the Joint State Public Service Commission (JSPSC) classified as a statutory body and NOT 
    a constitutional body?
A4. Under Article 315(2), a JSPSC is created by an ACT OF PARLIAMENT upon the request of the concerned 
    State Legislatures, rather than being created directly by the text of the Constitution.

Q5. Does the Attorney General of India have the right to vote when attending a parliamentary committee 
    of which he is named a member?
A5. No. Under Article 88, the Attorney General has the right to speak and take part in the proceedings 
    of either House, any joint sitting, and any committee of Parliament, but is EXPLICITLY BARRED 
    from the right to vote.

---d7:T1696,Non-constitutional public institutions in India fall into two broad structural classes:
1. **Statutory Bodies**: Established by an **Act of Parliament**. They derive their powers, mandate, and autonomy from parent legislation (e.g., NHRC, CIC, CVC, Lokpal, NIA, NDMA).
2. **Executive (Non-Statutory / Extra-Constitutional) Bodies**: Created by an **executive order or resolution of the Union Cabinet**. They have no constitutional base and no statutory parent act (e.g., NITI Aayog, Law Commission).

---d8:T1312,### A. Genesis & Departure from the Planning Commission
- Established on **January 1, 2015** by a Cabinet Resolution, replacing the 65-year-old **Planning Commission** (set up in March 1950).
- **Core Philosophy**: Shift from a centralized, top-down, command-and-control Soviet model of "one-size-fits-all" planning to **Cooperative Federalism** and **Competitive Federalism** ("Team India").

---

### B. Composition & Organisational Framework
- **Chairperson**: **Prime Minister of India**.
- **Governing Council**: Chief Ministers of all States, Chief Ministers of UTs with legislative assemblies (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K), and Lieutenant Governors of other UTs.
- **Regional Councils**: Convened to address specific inter-state or regional contingencies; chaired by PM or his nominee.
- **Vice-Chairperson**: Appointed by the PM; enjoys the rank of a **Cabinet Minister**.
- **Full-Time Members**: Enjoy the rank of a **Minister of State**.
- **Part-Time Members**: Maximum of 2 members from leading universities and research organizations in an *ex-officio* capacity.
- **Ex-Officio Members**: Maximum of 4 members of the Union Council of Ministers nominated by the PM.
- **Chief Executive Officer (CEO)**: Appointed by the PM for a fixed tenure; holds the rank of **Secretary to the Government of India**.
- **Attached Specialized Wings**:
  1. *Atal Innovation Mission (AIM)*: Cultivates entrepreneurship and tinkering labs across schools.
  2. *Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office (DMEO)*: Monitors output-outcome frameworks of central schemes.

---d9:T1185,### A. Statutory Base & Composition (2019 Amendments)
Established under the *Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993* (PHRA) to safeguard human rights defined as life, liberty, equality, and dignity guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in International Covenants.
- **Composition (under PHRA Amendment Act, 2019)**:
  - **Chairperson**: Has been a **Chief Justice of India OR a Judge of the Supreme Court**.
  - **Members (5 Whole-Time)**:
    - 1 Member who is or has been a **Judge of the Supreme Court**.
    - 1 Member who is or has been the **Chief Justice of a High Court**.
    - 3 Members having knowledge of human rights, **at least one of whom MUST BE A WOMAN**.
  - **Ex-Officio Members (7)**: Chairpersons of NCSC, NCST, NCBC, National Commission for Women (NCW), National Commission for Minorities, NCPCR (Child Rights), and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities.

---

### C. Powers & Critical Functional Limitations
1. **Civil Court Powers**: Enjoys all powers of a civil court trying a suit under the CPC: summoning witnesses, discovery of documents, requisitioning public records.
2. **RECOMMENDATORY CHARACTER**:
   - The NHRC has **no power to punish the violators of human rights**, nor to award monetary relief to the victim directly.
   - Its recommendations are **purely advisory**. The concerned government must inform the commission of action taken within **one month**.
3. **Statutory Limitation Period**: Cannot inquire into any matter after the expiration of **ONE (1) YEAR** from the date on which the human rights violation occurred (**Section 36(2)**).
4. **Armed Forces Barrier**: When investigating human rights violations by the Armed Forces, NHRC cannot investigate directly; it can only seek a factual report from the Central Government.

---da:Td97,### A. Statutory Base & Composition (RTI Act, 2005)
Established under the *Right to Information Act, 2005*.
- **Composition**: Chief Information Commissioner (CIC) and not more than **ten (10) Information Commissioners (ICs)**.
- **Selection Committee (3 Members)**:
  1. Prime Minister (Chairperson)
  2. Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha
  3. A Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister.

---

---db:T557,### A. Origin & Statutory Evolution
- Set up in **1964** on the recommendations of the **K. Santhanam Committee on Prevention of Corruption (1962–64)** as an apex vigilance institution.
- Conferred **statutory status** via the *Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003* pursuant to the Supreme Court's directives in the landmark ***Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1998)*** judgment.

---

### B. Composition, Unique Tenure & Selection (CVC Act, 2003)
- **Composition**: Central Vigilance Commissioner (Chairperson) + not more than **two (2) Vigilance Commissioners**.
- **Selection Committee (3 Members)**:
  1. **Prime Minister** (Chairperson)
  2. **Union Minister of Home Affairs**
  3. **Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha** (or leader of single largest opposition party).
- **The Unique 4-Year Tenure**:
  $$\text{Tenure of CVC: } \mathbf{FOUR\text{ (4) YEARS}} \text{ or until attaining the age of } \mathbf{65\text{ YEARS}}, \text{ whichever is earlier.}$$
- **Post-Tenure Ban**: On ceasing to hold office, the CVC and Commissioners are **ineligible for further employment** under the Government of India or any State.
- **Supervisory Authority**: Exercises superintendence over the functioning of the **Delhi Special Police Establishment (CBI)** in so far as it relates to the investigation of offences under the *Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988*.

---dc:Tfe8,### A. Genesis of the Ombudsman Concept
- Concept originated in **Sweden in 1809** (Ombudsman = grievance redressal agent).
- Term *"Lokpal"* was coined by **Dr. L.M. Singhvi** in 1963.
- First Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC, 1966) recommended the creation of a two-tier anti-corruption ombudsman: Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayukta in the States.
- Enacted as ***The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013*** following the Anna Hazare anti-corruption movement.

---

### B. Jurisdiction & Purview of the Lokpal
The Lokpal has anti-corruption jurisdiction over:
1. **Prime Minister of India**: Subject to strict safeguards—allegations relating to *international relations, external and internal security, public order, atomic energy, and space* are **exempted** from Lokpal inquiry. Inquiry must be held *in-camera*, and must be approved by **two-thirds of the full bench of the Lokpal**.
2. **Union Ministers & Members of Parliament**: (Excludes votes given or speeches delivered in Parliament under Article 105).
3. **Public Servants**: All Group A, B, C, and D officers of the Central Government.
4. **NGOs & Trusts**: Directors and managers of entities receiving government funding or foreign contributions exceeding **₹10 Lakh per annum** under FCRA.

---

### C. Composition & High-Powered Selection Committee

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

```

> [!NOTE]
> **State Lokayuktas**:
> **Maharashtra** was the first state to establish a Lokayukta in **1971** (Odisha passed the Act first in 1970 but established it in 1983). Under the 2013 Act, every State is legally mandated to establish a Lokayukta within one year.

---dd:T7e8,### A. Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)
- Set up in **1963** by a Resolution of the Ministry of Home Affairs; later transferred to the **Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (DoPT)**.
- **Not a Statutory Body**: CBI is not created by an Act of Parliament; it derives its police investigating powers from the ***Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946***.
- **Director of CBI**:
  - Tenure: Fixed minimum tenure of **2 years** under the CVC Act 2003 (*Vineet Narain*).
  - *2021 DSPE Amendment*: Allowed government to extend tenure of CBI Director up to **5 years** (one year at a time).
  - *Selection Committee*: (1) Prime Minister, (2) Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, (3) Chief Justice of India (or nominee).
- **State Consent Dynamics (§6 DSPE Act)**:
  - CBI **cannot** investigate offences in a State without the consent of that State Government.
  - *General Consent vs. Specific Consent*: Many states have withdrawn "General Consent", requiring CBI to seek case-by-case permission.
  - *Exception*: Supreme Court and High Courts can direct CBI to investigate any crime anywhere in India **without the consent of the State** (*State of West Bengal v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights, 2010*).

---

### B. National Investigation Agency (NIA)
- Established under the ***National Investigation Agency Act, 2008*** post-26/11 Mumbai terror attacks.
- India's premier **central counter-terrorism agency**.
- **No State Consent Required**: Unlike the CBI, the NIA possesses **sovereign statutory power to enter any State and investigate scheduled terror offences WITHOUT obtaining prior consent from the State Government**.
- **2019 NIA Amendment Act Expansions**:
  1. Jurisdiction expanded to investigate: Human trafficking, counterfeit currency, cyber-terrorism, and offences under the Explosive Substances Act.
  2. Extra-territorial jurisdiction: Empowered to investigate offences committed **outside India** affecting Indian citizens or Indian interests abroad.

---df:T7d1,```
Q1. What is the fundamental difference between the statutory status of the National Investigation 
    Agency (NIA) and the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)?
A1. The NIA is a full-fledged statutory body created directly by the NIA Act, 2008, and needs no 
    state consent to investigate terror crimes. The CBI is NOT a statutory body (created by executive 
    resolution in 1963) and derives its police powers from the DSPE Act, 1946; it requires state consent 
    under Section 6 unless directed by the SC or HC.

Q2. What is the unique tenure prescribed for the Central Vigilance Commissioner (CVC) under the CVC Act?
A2. A unique term of FOUR (4) YEARS or until attaining the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. 
    (Almost all other statutory bodies feature 3-year or 5-year terms).

Q3. What changes did the 2019 Amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act make regarding the 
    eligibility of the NHRC Chairperson?
A3. Earlier, only a retired Chief Justice of India was eligible. The 2019 amendment made a retired 
    Judge of the Supreme Court ALSO eligible to be appointed as Chairperson of the NHRC, and reduced 
    the tenure from 5 years to 3 years.

Q4. Under what constitutional or statutory power did NITI Aayog lose the authority to allocate central 
    plan funds to the States?
A4. The Planning Commission had acquired extra-constitutional fund allocation powers under Article 282 
    grants. NITI Aayog was conceptualized purely as a policy think-tank and catalyst; its founding 
    cabinet resolution in 2015 explicitly removed fund allocation powers and restored that authority 
    to the Union Ministry of Finance.

Q5. Who co-chairs the District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA) under the Disaster Management Act, 2005?
A5. The District Collector / District Magistrate serves as Chairperson, and the elected Chairperson 
    of the Zilla Parishad serves as the Co-Chairperson (blending administrative command with democratic 
    legitimacy).

---e1:Ta02,The original Constitution of 1950 did not contain any specific provisions for administrative tribunals. As the administrative welfare state expanded, conventional civil courts were overwhelmed by docket explosion and lacked specialized technical expertise.
- **The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976**:
  Inserted **Part XIV-A** into the Constitution, consisting of two foundational articles:
  1. **Article 323A**: Administrative Tribunals (public service disputes).
  2. **Article 323B**: Tribunals for Other Matters (taxation, foreign exchange, industrial disputes, land reforms, elections to local bodies, etc.).

---e3:T9a6,### A. Genesis & Jurisdiction (Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985)
- Established in **1985** under Article 323A. Principal Bench at **New Delhi** with **19 regular benches** operating across India.
- **Jurisdiction**: Adjudicates recruitment and service conditions of:
  1. Members of the **All India Services** (IAS, IPS, IFS).
  2. Members of the **Central Civil Services** and holders of civil posts under the Union.
  3. Civilian employees of the **Defence Services**.
- **Entities Excluded from CAT Jurisdiction**:
  - Members of the **Armed Forces (Military)**.
  - Officers and servants of the **Supreme Court and High Courts**.
  - Secretariat staff of **both Houses of Parliament**.

---

### B. Composition & Guiding Principles
- Consists of a **Chairman** and both **Judicial and Administrative Members**.
- Appointed by the **President of India** on the recommendations of a High-Powered Search-cum-Selection Committee chaired by the **Chief Justice of India (or a Supreme Court Judge nominated by CJI)**.
- **Exemption from Technical CPC Procedures**:
  The CAT is **not bound by the strict procedure laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908**. It is guided by the **Principles of Natural Justice**. Nominal application fee of **₹50** ensures low-cost, accessible justice.

---

### C. The Historic Jurisprudential Shift: *L. Chandra Kumar (1997)*
The constitutional validity and jurisdiction of tribunals underwent a complete transformation:
- ***S.P. Sampath Kumar v. Union of India (1987)***: A 5-judge bench initially held that tribunals were an "effective alternative institutional mechanism" to High Courts, upholding the statutory exclusion of High Court writ review under Articles 226/227.
- ***L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)* (7-Judge Constitution Bench)**:
  1. Overruled *Sampath Kumar*.
  2. Declared that the power of judicial review vested in the High Courts under **Articles 226/227** and the Supreme Court under **Article 32** is an **INVIOLABLE PART OF THE BASIC STRUCTURE OF THE CONSTITUTION**.
  3. Struck down Clause 2(d) of Article 323A and Clause 3(d) of Article 323B which excluded High Court jurisdiction.
  4. **The Modern Operational Rule**: Tribunals act as **courts of first instance**. An aggrieved party **cannot approach the Supreme Court directly under Article 136**; they must first appeal against the Tribunal's decision before a **Division Bench of the concerned High Court under Article 226/227**.

---e4:T131c,### A. Statutory Base & Global Precedence
- Established in **2010** under the ***National Green Tribunal Act, 2010***, drawing legitimacy from **Article 21** (Right to a healthy and clean environment).
- Made India the **third country in the world** (after Australia and New Zealand) to establish a specialized environmental tribunal, and the first developing nation to do so.
- **Principal Bench**: **New Delhi**; Zonal Benches at **Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, and Chennai**.

---

### B. Mandate, Composition & Guiding Principles
- **Mandatory Disposal Timeline**: Mandated by Section 18 to dispose of applications and appeals finally within **SIX (6) MONTHS** of filing.
- **Composition**: Full-time Chairperson (retired SC Judge or retired HC Chief Justice) + minimum 10 and maximum 20 Judicial Members + minimum 10 and maximum 20 Expert Members.
- **Guiding Principles (Section 20)**:
  Not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure (1908) or Indian Evidence Act (1872). Governed by Principles of Natural Justice and must apply:
  1. **The Polluter Pays Principle**
  2. **The Precautionary Principle**
  3. **The Principle of Sustainable Development & Inter-generational Equity**

---e7:T700,```
Q1. Which constitutional amendment added Part XIV-A (Tribunals) to the Constitution of India, and 
    on the recommendation of which committee?
A1. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, inserted Part XIV-A (Articles 323A and 323B) on the 
    recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.

Q2. What did the 7-judge Constitution Bench rule in L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) regarding 
    the jurisdiction of High Courts over tribunals?
A2. The Supreme Court struck down provisions excluding High Court review, holding that the power of 
    judicial review under Articles 226/227 and 32 is an untruncatable part of the Basic Structure. 
    Tribunals act as courts of first instance; their decisions must be challenged before a Division 
    Bench of the High Court before appealing to the Supreme Court.

Q3. Name two prominent environmental statutes that are strictly EXCLUDED from the jurisdiction of 
    the National Green Tribunal (NGT).
A3. (1) The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, and (2) The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest 
    Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) / Indian Forest Act, 1927.

Q4. What is the fundamental difference in legislative competence between Article 323A and Article 323B?
A4. Under Article 323A, administrative tribunals can be established ONLY BY PARLIAMENT. Under Article 
    323B, tribunals for other specified matters can be established by BOTH PARLIAMENT AND STATE 
    LEGISLATURES within their respective legislative competencies.

Q5. What is the statutory time limit within which the National Green Tribunal is mandated to dispose 
    of environmental disputes?
A5. Exactly SIX (6) MONTHS from the date of filing of the application or appeal (Section 18(5) of the 
    NGT Act, 2010).

---e9:T431,In a democratic republic governed by the rule of law, secrecy in public affairs is the exception, and openness is the foundational rule.
- **Constitutional Pedigree**: The Right to Information is not explicitly enumerated in Part III of the Constitution, but was judicialized as an **integral facet of Article 19(1)(a)** (Freedom of Speech and Expression) and **Article 21** (Right to Life and Liberty).
- ***State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975)* (Justice K.K. Mathew)**:
  > *"In a government of responsibility like ours, where all the agents of the public must be responsible for their conduct, there can be but few secrets. The people of this country have a right to know every public act, everything that is done in a public way, by their public functionaries."*
- **Grassroots Revolution**: The movement for a statutory right was catalyzed in the 1990s by the **Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS)** led by **Aruna Roy** in rural Rajasthan, demanding access to muster rolls and bills under the battle cry: *"Hamara Paisa, Hamara Hisab"* (Our Money, Our Accounts).

---ea:T3f0d,Enacted on June 15, 2005, the **RTI Act, 2005 came into full force on October 12, 2005**. It dismantled the colonial culture of administrative opacity.

### A. Definition of "Public Authority" (Section 2(h))
A Public Authority means any authority, body, or institution of self-government established or constituted:
1. By or under the **Constitution**.
2. By any other law made by **Parliament**.
3. By any other law made by **State Legislature**.
4. By notification issued or order made by the appropriate Government, including:
   - Any body **owned, controlled, or substantially financed** by government funds.
   - Non-Government Organizations (NGOs) **substantially financed, directly or indirectly**, by funds provided by the appropriate Government.

---

### B. Statutory Timelines for Information Delivery (Section 7)

├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Section 8(1)(j)    │ Personal information having no relationship to public activity/interest, or │
│                    │ which causes unwarranted invasion of individual privacy.                    │
└────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The Public Interest Override (Section 8(2))**:
> Notwithstanding anything in the Official Secrets Act, 1923, nor any of the exemptions permissible under Section 8(1), a public authority **may allow access to information if public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interests**.
> **The 20-Year Rule (Section 8(3))**: Any information relating to an event or matter which occurred **twenty (20) years** before the date of the request must be disclosed (excluding clauses (a), (c), and (i)).

### D. Exempted Organizations (Section 24)
- Intelligence and security organizations specified in the **Second Schedule** (IB, RAW, Directorate of Revenue Intelligence, Central Economic Intelligence Bureau, Enforcement Directorate, BSF, CRPF, ITBP, CISF, NSG, Assam Rifles, Special Frontier Force) are **exempted from the Act**.
- > [!WARNING]
  > **EXAM TRAP: The Corruption & Human Rights Exception to Section 24**
  > Information pertaining to **ALLEGATIONS OF CORRUPTION AND HUMAN RIGHTS VIOLATIONS is NOT EXEMPT** from disclosure even in these security agencies!
  > Allegations of human rights violations can be disclosed only with the approval of the Central Information Commission within **45 days**.

---eb:T40b,The **Official Secrets Act, 1923** was enacted by Lord Curzon's administration to consolidate British colonial laws relating to state espionage.
- **Section 3**: Penalizes spying, approaching prohibited military areas, or sketching sensitive fortifications.
- **Section 5 (The Catch-All Draconian Clause)**: Makes the unauthorized communication, retention, or receipt of *any official secret, secret document, or code* a punishable criminal offence. The term *"Official Secret"* is **nowhere defined** in the Act, leaving total discretion to bureaucrats to stamp any routine file "Secret" or "Confidential".

### The Supremacy Clause: Section 22 of the RTI Act, 2005
Section 22 provides an absolute non-obstante clause establishing the supremacy of citizen transparency over colonial secrecy:
$$\text{SECTION 22: The provisions of the RTI Act } \mathbf{SHALL\text{ HAVE EFFECT NOTWITHSTANDING ANYTHING INCONSISTENT}}$$
$$\text{therewith contained in the Official Secrets Act, 1923, or any other law for the time being in force.}$$

Q1. Under what constitutional article is the Right to Information primarily grounded as an implied 
    fundamental right?
A1. Under Article 19(1)(a) (Freedom of Speech and Expression), as affirmed in State of U.P. v. Raj 
    Narain (1975) and S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981).

Q2. What is the mandatory statutory timeframe under Section 7(1) of the RTI Act for providing information 
    that concerns the "Life or Liberty" of a person?
A2. Exactly FORTY-EIGHT (48) HOURS from the time of receipt of the application.

Q3. Does the Official Secrets Act, 1923 override the Right to Information Act, 2005 in case of conflict?
A3. No. Under Section 22 of the RTI Act, 2005, the provisions of the RTI Act have an explicit OVERRIDING 
    EFFECT notwithstanding anything inconsistent contained in the Official Secrets Act, 1923, or any 
    other law.

Q4. Are intelligence agencies like the Intelligence Bureau (IB) and RAW completely immune from all 
    RTI queries under Section 24?
A4. No. Under the provisos to Section 24(1), information pertaining to ALLEGATIONS OF CORRUPTION AND 
    HUMAN RIGHTS VIOLATIONS is NOT exempt from disclosure.

Q5. What is the maximum statutory penalty that the Central Information Commission can impose on a 
    Public Information Officer (PIO) under Section 20 of the RTI Act?
A5. A fine of ₹250 per day up to a MAXIMUM OF ₹25,000, in addition to recommending disciplinary action 
    under applicable service rules.

---f0:T9e1,Political theory is the systematic inquiry into the values, principles, institutions, and practices that organize collective human life. It operates on two interrelated axes:
1. **Normative Theory**: Evaluates what *ought* to be—interrogating ideals of justice, moral legitimacy, human freedom, and ethical obligation (Plato, Kant, Rawls).
2. **Empirical Theory**: Analyzes what *is*—systematically explaining institutional mechanics, voting behaviors, power relations, and governance outputs (Machiavelli, Weber, Dahl).

---f1:T1350,Liberty constitutes the bedrock of constitutional democracy and liberal thought. The modern taxonomy pivots upon the distinction formulated by **Sir Isaiah Berlin** in his seminal lecture *Two Concepts of Liberty* (1958).

### J.S. Mill’s Harm Principle (*On Liberty*, 1859)
John Stuart Mill defended liberty on utilitarian and developmental grounds, articulating the canonical boundary between individual autonomy and state intervention:
- **The Sole End of Intervention**: *"The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant."*
- **Self-Regarding Actions**: Actions affecting solely the individual (e.g., diet, personal belief, reading). Society has **zero coercive jurisdiction**, even if the act is harmful to the self.
- **Other-Regarding Actions**: Actions affecting the interests or rights of third parties (e.g., violence, theft, public nuisance). The state is legitimately entitled to regulate or punish.

---f2:T8f6,Equality does not mean identity of treatment or equalizing physical characteristics; it mandates that no person shall suffer arbitrary discrimination and that all persons possess equal moral worth.

### A. Dimensions of Equality
1. **Formal / Legal Equality**: Equality before the law and equal protection of the laws (Dicey's Rule of Law; Article 14 of the Indian Constitution).
2. **Political Equality**: Equal political voice (*"One person, one vote, one value"*; Universal adult suffrage; Article 326).
3. **Equality of Opportunity**:
   - *Formal Equality of Opportunity*: Careers open to talents without hereditary, caste, or religious bars.
   - *Fair Equality of Opportunity (Substantive)*: Leveling the starting line through education, nutrition, and affirmative action so that structural disadvantages are neutralized before competition begins.
4. **Equality of Outcome / Condition**: Ensuring socio-economic results are equalized (advocated by radical socialists and Marxists; rejected by classical liberals as incompatible with freedom).

### B. Ronald Dworkin: Equality of Resources
- Ronald Dworkin argued in *Sovereign Virtue* (2000) that justice requires **treating individuals as equals**, meaning the state must show equal concern and respect.
- **Ambition-Sensitive vs. Endowment-Insensitive**:
  - *Endowment-Insensitive*: Distribution should not be determined by brute luck (genetic intelligence, inherited wealth, physical disability). Society must compensate for these arbitrary disadvantages.
  - *Ambition-Sensitive*: Distribution should reflect people's conscious choices, work ethic, and lifestyle preferences (option luck). If someone chooses leisure over income, the difference in wealth is legitimate.

### C. Amartya Sen & Martha Nussbaum: The Capability Approach
- **Critique of Resourcism & Utilitarianism**: Giving two people the exact same income or bundle of primary goods does not make them equal if one is healthy and the other has a chronic illness.
- **Functionings**: Beings and doings that people value (being nourished, educated, sheltered, having self-respect).
- **Capabilities**: The substantive freedom or real opportunity a person possesses to achieve various functionings. Poverty is not merely low income; it is **capability deprivation**.

---f3:T16e3,Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought (John Rawls). The central modern dispute concerns whether justice is distributive (patterned) or historical (procedural).

```
                                  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                                  │      THE ARCHITECTURE OF JUSTICE THEORIES     │
                                  └──────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                                                         │
                ┌────────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────┐
                ▼                                                                                 ▼
   ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐                       ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │       EGALITARIAN LIBERALISM           │                       │             LIBERTARIANISM             │
   │       John Rawls (1921–2002)           │                       │        Robert Nozick (1938–2002)       │
   │  *A Theory of Justice* (1971)          │                       │     *Anarchy, State, and Utopia* (1974)│
   ├────────────────────────────────────────┤                       ├────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ • Justice as Fairness                  │                       │ • Entitlement Theory of Justice        │
   │ • Original Position + Veil of Ignorance│                       │ • Historical, Non-patterned Principle  │
   │ • Difference Principle (Maximin)       │                       │ • Self-ownership & Absolute Property   │
   │ • Reconciles Freedom with Equality     │                       │ • "Taxation of earnings is forced labor│
   └────────────────────────────────────────┘                       └────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### A. John Rawls: *Justice as Fairness*
Rawls revived the social contract tradition to defeat utilitarianism (which sacrifices minority rights for aggregate social utility).

1. **The Original Position & Veil of Ignorance**:
   - Hypothetical deliberative setup where rational representatives choose the basic principles of society.
   - The participants are enveloped in a **"Veil of Ignorance"**: they do not know their race, caste, sex, wealth, intelligence, physical strength, or personal conception of the good life.
   - Operating under uncertainty, rational agents adopt the **Maximin Rule** (maximizing the minimum position) to ensure that if they wake up at the absolute bottom of society, their conditions are as favorable as possible.

2. **The Two Principles of Justice (Lexical Order)**:
   - **First Principle (Equal Liberty Principle)**: Each person has an equal right to the most extensive scheme of equal basic liberties compatible with a similar system of liberty for all. (Strict lexical priority over economic gains).
   - **Second Principle (Social and Economic Inequalities)**: They must satisfy two conditions:
     - *(a) Fair Equality of Opportunity*: Offices and positions must be open to all under conditions of fair opportunity.
     - *(b) The Difference Principle*: Inequalities are justified **only if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society**.

### B. Robert Nozick: The Entitlement Theory of Justice
Robert Nozick presented the libertarian antithesis to Rawls, defending self-ownership:
1. **Self-Ownership Thesis**: Individuals own themselves, their talents, and their labor. Any involuntary redistribution violates Kant’s imperative never to treat persons merely as means to an end.
2. **Three Principles of Just Holdings**:
   - **Principle of Justice in Acquisition**: Initial appropriation of unowned resources is just if it does not leave others worse off (Lockean proviso).
   - **Principle of Justice in Transfer**: Voluntary market exchanges, gifts, and contracts without fraud or coercion produce just distributions.
   - **Principle of Rectification of Injustice**: Correcting historical violations of the first two principles.
3. **No-Pattern Thesis**: *"Liberty upsets patterns."* Any attempt to impose an end-state distribution (like Rawls' Difference Principle or socialist equality) requires continuous, tyrannical state interference into private lives.

### C. Communitarian & Post-Colonial Critiques
- **Michael Sandel (*Liberalism and the Limits of Justice*, 1982)**: Criticized Rawls' "unencumbered self." Human beings are embedded in communities, traditions, and historical identities; we cannot deliberate in an atomized vacuum.
- **Amartya Sen (*The Idea of Justice*, 2009)**: Distinguished between **Niti** (institutional correctness, organizational rules) and **Nyaya** (realized justice, actual lives lived). Rawls focuses exclusively on *Niti* (ideal institutional blueprints), whereas justice demands addressing remediable injustices in the real world (*Nyaya*).

### Austinian Classical Sovereignty
John Austin (*The Province of Jurisprudence Determined*, 1832) defined sovereignty:
> *"If a determinate human superior, not in a habit of obedience to a like superior, receive habitual obedience from the bulk of a given society, that determinate superior is sovereign in that society, and the society (including the superior) is a society political and independent."*
- **Four Cardinal Attributes**: Absoluteness, Universality, Inalienability, Indivisibility.
- **Constitutional Reality**: In modern constitutional federations (like India and the USA), Austinian sovereignty is a legal fiction. Sovereignty is **divided between Union and States**, limited by **Fundamental Rights (Part III)**, and circumscribed by **Judicial Review (Basic Structure Doctrine)**.

---f7:Te96,```

├─────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤

---f8:T5cc,> [!WARNING]
> **Trap 1: J.S. Mill Did Not Advocate Unconditional Universal Franchise**  
> Prelims questions often claim Mill supported complete, equal adult franchise. In truth, Mill in *Considerations on Representative Government* (1861) advocated **weighted/plural voting** for educated citizens and disqualified those who could not read, write, or pay taxes, fearing the "tyranny of the uneducated majority."

> [!WARNING]
> **Trap 2: Rawls Does Not Mandate Absolute Economic Equality**  
> Candidates frequently confuse Rawls' Difference Principle with egalitarian communism. Rawls explicitly permits wide economic disparities, provided those disparities create incentives that improve the material conditions of the least advantaged class compared to equality.

> [!WARNING]
> **Trap 3: Berlin's Critique of Positive Liberty Was Not a Denial of Its Moral Value**  
> Berlin recognized positive liberty as a valid human ideal, but cautioned that historically, totalitarian states (Jacobins, Stalinism, Fascism) perverted "self-mastery" into authoritarian state coercion by claiming the State represents the "true" or "higher" self of the citizen.

> [!WARNING]
> **Trap 4: Austinian Sovereignty Does Not Exist in Federal Constitutions**  
> Austin insisted that sovereignty is indivisible. In a federation (such as India or the US), power is constitutionally bifurcated between the Union and the States; thus, monistic sovereignty collapses under federal constitutionalism.

---f9:T51c,1. **Analytical Mechanics**: Explain how John Rawls' "Veil of Ignorance" eliminates arbitrary natural endowments from the determination of principles of justice.
2. **Comparative Critique**: Contrast Robert Nozick's Entitlement Theory with Rawls' Difference Principle. Why does Nozick claim that patterned distributions violate individual liberty?
3. **Jurisprudential Application**: How does the Indian Supreme Court's jurisprudence on Article 21 (Right to Livelihood, Right to Privacy in *Puttaswamy*) represent a transition from Negative Liberty to Positive Liberty?
4. **Institutional Inquiry**: Why did Harold Laski argue that *"because society is federal, authority must also be federal"*? Critically evaluate this against John Austin's monistic model.
5. **Democratic Models**: Contrast Joseph Schumpeter's Elitist model of democracy with Jürgen Habermas' Deliberative model. What role does citizen rationality play in each?

---fb:T972,An ideology is a coherent set of ideas, beliefs, and values that provides:
1. **A Diagnostic Worldview**: An explanatory critique of the existing social, political, and economic order.
2. **A Normative Vision**: A desired future model of the good society.
3. **An Action-Oriented Program**: A strategic pathway (reform, evolution, revolution, or non-violent resistance) to achieve that desired transformation.

### Key Conceptual Pillars
- **Individualism**: The individual is the primary moral unit with intrinsic worth, prior to and independent of society.
- **Reason & Rationality**: Belief in human capacity to resolve conflicts through debate, law, and contractual agreement rather than dogma or violence.
- **Constitutionalism & Limited Government**: Distrust of concentrated sovereign power (Montesquieu's separation of powers, Locke's trust model, Lord Acton: *"Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely"*).

---fd:Tf72,Socialism emerged as a moral and economic critique of industrial capitalism, prioritizing **community, social equality, cooperation, and collective provision** over unfettered competition and private profit.

### Democratic Socialism in the Indian Constitutional Context
- **Nehruvian Synthesis**: Jawaharlal Nehru rejected the coercive, violent methods of Soviet Marxism while embracing socialist planning. He championed a **"Mixed Economy"** where the public sector controlled the *"commanding heights of the economy"* while permitting regulated private enterprise.
- **Constitutional Expression**:
  - **Preamble**: "Socialist" added by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976**.
  - **Directive Principles of State Policy**: **Article 39(b)** (distribution of material resources to subserve common good) and **Article 39(c)** (prevention of concentration of wealth).
  - ***Excel Wear v. Union of India (1978)* & *D.S. Nakara v. Union of India (1983)***: The Supreme Court held that Indian socialism is a blend of Marxism and Gandhian philosophy, leaning heavily towards Gandhian socialism—striving to eliminate inequalities in income, status, and opportunity without abolishing private property entirely.

---fe:T149c,Karl Marx (1818–1883) and Friedrich Engels (1820–1895) formulated "Scientific Socialism," rooting political theory in economic reality, historical contradictions, and class dynamics.

### A. Four Core Pillars of Classical Marxism
1. **Historical Materialism**: History progresses through distinct modes of production driven by contradictions between the *Forces of Production* and the *Relations of Production*:
   $$\text{Primitive Communism} \longrightarrow \text{Slavery} \longrightarrow \text{Feudalism} \longrightarrow \text{Capitalism} \longrightarrow \text{Socialism} \longrightarrow \text{Communism}$$
2. **Theory of Surplus Value (*Das Kapital*, 1867)**: The value of a commodity is determined by the socially necessary labor-time to produce it. The capitalist pays the worker only subsistence wages; the difference between the total value produced and the wage paid is **Surplus Value**, which is expropriated as capitalist profit.
3. **Theory of Alienation (*Economic & Philosophic Manuscripts*, 1844)**: Under capitalism, the worker is estranged on four levels:
   - Alienation from the **product** of labor (it belongs to the capitalist).
   - Alienation from the **act of production** (work is repetitive, coercive drudgery).
   - Alienation from **human nature / species-essence (*Gattungswesen*)** (creativity is stifled).
   - Alienation from **other human beings** (colleagues become competitors).
4. **State as an Instrument of Class Oppression**:
   - The state is not a neutral arbiter. In *The Communist Manifesto* (1848): *"The executive of the modern state is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie."*
   - **Withering Away of the State**: Following the proletarian revolution, a temporary transitional phase (*Dictatorship of the Proletariat*) dismantles capitalist resistance. Once classes are eradicated, the state loses its coercive function and naturally **withers away**.

---ff:Tef2,Twentieth-century Western Marxists abandoned crude economic determinism to explain why capitalism survived and did not collapse as Marx had predicted.

---100:T10bf,Mahatma Gandhi (1869–1948) developed an indigenous, deeply moral philosophy that rejected Western modernity, statism, and violent revolution.

```
                                  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                                  │      THE ARCHITECTURE OF GANDHIAN THOUGHT     │
                                  └──────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘

                ┌──────────────────┬─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
                ▼                  ▼                     ▼                     ▼                  ▼
        ┌───────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐     ┌───────────────┐     ┌───────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐
        │  SATYAGRAHA   │  │   SARVODAYA   │     │  TRUSTEESHIP  │     │    SWARAJ     │  │OCEANIC CIRCLES│
        │ Truth-Force & │  │ Welfare of all│     │ Moral Social- │     │ Self-rule and │  │Decentralized  │
        │ Ahimsa (Soul- │  │ (Not greatest │     │ ism; Wealthy  │     │ Self-restraint│  │Village Repub- │
        │ Force)        │  │ good of number│     │ hold in trust │     │ (Hind Swaraj) │  │lics (No Apex) │
        └───────────────┘  └───────────────┘     └───────────────┘     └───────────────┘  └───────────────┘
```

### A. Satyagraha & Ahimsa (Non-Violence)
- **Satyagraha**: Literal meaning: *"Holding onto Truth."* It is not passive resistance or the weapon of the weak; it is active soul-force.
- **Means and Ends Continuity**: Gandhi adamantly rejected Machiavellian or Marxist doctrines that *"the ends justify the means."* To Gandhi:
  > *"The means may be likened to a seed, the end to a tree; and there is just the same inviolable connection between the means and the end as there is between the seed and the tree."* Impure means irrevocably corrupt the end.

### B. Sarvodaya vs. Utilitarianism
- Inspired by John Ruskin’s *Unto This Last*, Gandhi rejected Jeremy Bentham’s utilitarian doctrine of *"the greatest happiness of the greatest number"*, which permits the sacrifice of the minority.
- **Sarvodaya** means the **upliftment and welfare of all**, beginning with the poorest and most marginalized (*Antyodaya*).

### C. The Doctrine of Trusteeship
- Gandhi opposed the violent expropriation of capitalist property (Marxist expropriation) because violence destroys human soul and capacity.
- Capitalists and landlords must consider themselves not absolute owners, but **trustees** holding surplus wealth on behalf of society. They are entitled only to what is necessary for a modest livelihood; the rest belongs to the community.

### D. Swaraj & The Theory of Stateless Democracy ("Oceanic Circles")
- **Swaraj**: Means more than political independence from the British; it signifies **self-mastery, moral self-control, and spiritual autonomy** (*Hind Swaraj*, 1909).
- **Stateless Democracy / Enlightened Anarchy**: Gandhi viewed the modern state as an engine of organized and concentrated violence. In his ideal society, there is no coercive centralized state.
- **Oceanic Circles**: Power does not flow vertically in a pyramid (where the apex crushes the base), but radiates horizontally like concentric ripples in an ocean:
  > *"Life will not be a pyramid with the apex sustained by the bottom. But it will be an oceanic circle whose centre will be the individual always ready to perish for the village, the latter ready to perish for the circle of villages..."*

---102:T593,> [!WARNING]
> **Trap 1: Fabian Socialists Rejected Violent Revolution**  
> Prelims questions often conflate Fabian Socialism with Marxist Communism. Fabian Socialists (Sidney Webb, George Bernard Shaw) believed in the **"inevitability of gradualness"** through constitutional, parliamentary legislation and municipal governance, strictly repudiating armed revolution.

> [!WARNING]
> **Trap 2: Gandhi Was Philosophically an Anarchist, Not a Statonist**  
> Candidates frequently think Gandhi supported a powerful centralized welfare state. In political philosophy, Gandhi is classified as a **"Philosophical Anarchist"** who advocated a stateless society of decentralized self-sufficient village republics (*Gram Swaraj*).

> [!WARNING]
> **Trap 3: Gramsci Did Not Reject Marx's Economic Base**  
> Gramsci did not discard historical materialism; he supplemented it. He argued that economic crisis alone would not trigger revolution unless the working class dismantled the cultural and intellectual hegemony (*Egemonia*) of the bourgeoisie through a long-term "War of Position."

> [!WARNING]
> **Trap 4: Indian Constitutional Socialism Does Not Abolish Private Enterprise**  
> As ruled in *Excel Wear (1978)*, the word "Socialist" in the Preamble cannot be interpreted as converting India into a communist state where private ownership is prohibited; it mandates democratic social justice alongside private enterprise.

---103:T4ee,1. **Epistemological Analysis**: How did Antonio Gramsci's concept of "Hegemony" revolutionize Marxist political theory regarding the survival of capitalism in Western democracies?
2. **Philosophical Comparison**: Contrast Karl Marx's and Mahatma Gandhi's approaches to the state and property. Why did Gandhi propose "Trusteeship" over state expropriation?
3. **Ideological Evolution**: Trace the transformation of Liberalism from John Locke's "Night-watchman State" through T.H. Green's "Positive Liberty" to Friedrich Hayek's "Neo-Liberalism."
4. **Constitutional Application**: How does the Indian Constitution harmonize the tensions between Classical Liberalism (Fundamental Rights, Part III) and Democratic Socialism (DPSPs, Part IV)?
5. **Critique of Means and Ends**: Why did Gandhi assert that *"means are after all everything"*? Contrast this with the Leninist-Marxist doctrine of revolutionary transformation.

| **Fourth** | Allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) to States and Union Territories. | Articles 4(1) & 80(2) |
| **Fifth** | Administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes (Applicable to 10 States; TAC with up to 20 members). | Article 244(1) |
| **Sixth** | Administration of Tribal Areas in **AMTM** (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) via Autonomous District Councils (ADCs). | Articles 244(2) & 275(1) |
| **Seventh** | Division of legislative powers: Union List (100 items), State List (61 items), Concurrent List (52 items). | Article 246 |
| **Eighth** | 22 Officially Recognized Languages (Original 14; 21st, 71st, and 92nd Amendments added 8). | Articles 344(1) & 351 |
| **Ninth** | Validation of certain Acts and Regulations (Protected from judicial review before 1973; post-24 April 1973 laws subject to Basic Structure review per *I.R. Coelho*). | Article 31B |
| **Tenth** | Disqualification on grounds of Defection (Anti-Defection Law; added by 52nd AA 1985; strengthened by 91st AA 2003). | Articles 102(2) & 191(2) |
| **Eleventh** | Powers, authority, and functional responsibilities of Panchayats (**29 functional items**). | Article 243G |
| **Twelfth** | Powers, authority, and functional responsibilities of Municipalities (**18 functional items**). | Article 243W |

---106:Tcbf,| Amendment | Year | Strategic Constitutional Impact |
| :--- | :-: | :--- |
| **1st AA** | 1951 | Added 9th Schedule (Art 31B); inserted Art 15(4) for backward classes; restricted speech under Art 19(2) on grounds of public order, friendly foreign relations, and incitement. |
| **7th AA** | 1956 | States Reorganisation on linguistic basis; abolished Class A, B, C, D categories; enabled common High Courts; Governor can be appointed for 2+ States. |
| **24th AA** | 1971 | Affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution including Part III under Art 368; made President's assent to Constitutional Amendment Bills MANDATORY. |
| **42nd AA** | 1976 | "Mini-Constitution": Added "Socialist, Secular, Integrity" to Preamble; Part IV-A Fundamental Duties; Part XIV-A Tribunals; bound President to Cabinet advice (Art 74(1)); transferred 5 subjects from State to Concurrent List. |
| **44th AA** | 1978 | Undid 42nd distortions: Replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion" in Art 352; Arts 20 & 21 cannot be suspended during Emergency; deleted Right to Property from Part III (made legal right under Art 300A); Cabinet advice can be sent back ONCE for reconsideration; National Emergency requires WRITTEN Cabinet advice. |
| **52nd AA** | 1985 | Added Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law). |
| **61st AA** | 1988 | Lowered voting age from 21 years to 18 years in Article 326. |
| **73rd AA** | 1992 | Granted constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions (Part IX, 11th Schedule, 29 functional items). |
| **74th AA** | 1992 | Granted constitutional status to Urban Local Bodies (Part IX-A, 12th Schedule, 18 functional items). |
| **86th AA** | 2002 | Right to Education made Fundamental Right (Article 21A); amended Art 45; added 11th Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k). |
| **91st AA** | 2003 | Capped Council of Ministers to 15% of Lok Sabha / Vidhan Sabha strength (Min 12 in States); deleted 1/3rd split defense from 10th Schedule (only 2/3rd merger protected). |
| **99th AA** | 2014 | Established National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) — *Struck down by Supreme Court in 2015 as unconstitutional violation of judicial independence*. |
| **101st AA** | 2016 | Introduced Goods and Services Tax (GST); inserted Articles 246A, 269A, and created the GST Council under Article 279A. |
| **102nd AA** | 2018 | Granted constitutional status to National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) under Article 338B; inserted Article 342A. |
| **103rd AA** | 2019 | Introduced 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in education and public employment (Articles 15(6) and 16(6)). Upheld in *Janhit Abhiyan* (2022). |
| **104th AA** | 2020 | Extended reservation for SCs and STs in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies by 10 years (up to 2030); ceased reservation for Anglo-Indians (Articles 331 and 333). |
